text: Given an absolute Unix-style path, return its simplified canonical form. A single dot is the current directory, two dots is the parent, multiple slashes collapse to one, and the result starts with a slash and has no trailing slash unless it's root.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — only exactly two dots means parent; sequences like three dots or four dots are ordinary directory names. And a dot-dot at the root just stays at root. Right?
So I'll split on the slash first. After splitting, every segment is one of four things — empty, a dot, a dot-dot, or a name — and each maps to a simple action on a directory stack.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. Editing the string directly — deleting the segment before each dot-dot — is fiddly with all the slash edge cases. This problem reminds me of a stack used as an undo history: each name steps one level down, and a dot-dot undoes the most recent step, which is exactly last in, first out. So splitting into segments and pushing names onto a stack is cleaner: dot-dot pops, empty and dot are skipped, everything else pushes.

Here's the plan. One: split the path on the slash. Two: for each segment, dot-dot pops if the stack isn't empty, dot or empty is skipped, anything else is pushed. Three: join the stack with slashes, or return a single slash if it's empty. One thing worth flagging — I'll split with getline on a string stream, with the slash as the delimiter. The leading slash and consecutive slashes naturally produce empty segments, so collapsing multiple slashes falls out for free by skipping empties. And I match dot-dot as a whole string, so three dots stays a name. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I read segments with getline on a string stream, run the four cases against a stack of strings, and return a single slash when the stack ends up empty. One thing worth flagging — getline's third argument is the delimiter; without it, it defaults to newline and the whole path comes back as one chunk. And since a stack only exposes the top, I pop from the top and prepend each directory, so the answer still reads left to right.

Let's dry-run slash a, slash dot, slash b, slash dot-dot, slash dot-dot, slash c, slash. Expected: slash c. The rows that matter are the two dot-dots: they pop b, then a, back to root, and then c is pushed. The leading empty segment and the dot are skipped, and the trailing slash yields no segment at all, because getline stops at the end of the stream. Answer: slash c. That matches. Corner cases: slash dot-dot slash gives slash, since dot-dot on an empty stack is ignored. Slash three dots stays slash three dots, because three dots is a name. And slash home, double slash, foo, slash gives slash home slash foo, since the double slash just makes an empty segment.

The time complexity is linear for the split — one pass, with constant-time checks per segment. The space complexity is linear for the stack of segments. To be precise, prepending copies the partial answer every time, so the join can be quadratic in the worst case. Oh, one more thing — using a vector of strings instead of a stack makes the join a simple front-to-back concatenation, no prepending, and the whole thing truly linear.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You split first, so multiple and trailing slashes simply vanish. You matched dot-dot exactly, keeping three dots a valid name. And you guarded the pop at root and the empty-stack result. Good work.
